Root mean square speed comes from kinetic theory:
u(rms) = √(3RT/M)
At the same temperature 3RT is the same for every gas, so u(rms) ∝ 1/√M — the **lighter**
the gas, the faster its molecules.
Compare the molar masses:
CH₄ = 12 + 4 = 16 g mol⁻¹ ← lightest
CO = 12 + 16 = 28
CO₂ = 12 + 32 = 44
Cl₂ = 2 × 35.5 = 71 ← heaviest
Methane has the smallest M, so the largest u(rms).
As a check, the ratio of speeds for CH₄ and Cl₂ is √(71/16) ≈ 2.1, so methane molecules move
about twice as fast as chlorine molecules at the same temperature.
∴ CH₄.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|9||0|0.s:
Sodium couples the two carbons that carry the halogens — the Wurtz reaction. When both
halogens are in the same molecule the coupling is **intramolecular** and a ring closes.
Write out 1,4-dibromopentane:
C1       C2   C3   C4      C5
CH₂Br – CH₂ – CH₂ – CHBr – CH₃
Sodium removes both bromines and joins C1 to C4 directly.
The ring therefore contains C1, C2, C3 and C4 — four carbons, so a **cyclobutane** ring.
C5, the methyl group, was never attached to a bromine, so it stays as a substituent hanging
off C4.
That gives methylcyclobutane.
A useful check: count the ring size as (number of carbons between and including the two
halogen-bearing carbons) = 4, and anything beyond stays as a side chain.
∴ methyl cyclobutane.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|10||0|0.s:
The oxidising agent is the species that is **reduced**, so track the oxidation numbers.
2FeSO₄ + H₂SO₄ + H₂O₂ ⇒ Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + 2H₂O
Iron: +2 in FeSO₄ ⇒ +3 in Fe₂(SO₄)₃. It loses an electron, so iron is oxidised and FeSO₄ is the
reducing agent.
Oxygen in H₂O₂: the peroxide linkage gives each oxygen −1. In H₂O it is −2. So that oxygen
gains an electron — it is reduced.
Sulphuric acid: sulphur is +6 on both sides and oxygen −2 on both sides. Nothing changes, so
H₂SO₄ is only supplying the acidic medium, not taking part in the redox.
The species reduced is hydrogen peroxide, so it is the oxidising agent.
(H₂O₂ can act either way, since its oxygen at −1 sits between 0 and −2; here it goes down, so
it oxidises.)
∴ H₂O₂.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|11||0|0.s:
The equation given is the **formation** of two moles of water:
2H₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇒ 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −571.6 kJ
Decomposition is the reverse reaction, so reverse the sign:
2H₂O(l) ⇒ 2H₂(g) + O₂(g), ΔH = +571.6 kJ
But that is for two moles. The heat of decomposition is quoted **per mole**, so divide by 2:
H₂O(l) ⇒ H₂(g) + ½O₂(g), ΔH = +571.6/2 = +285.8 kJ
Both steps matter: the sign flips because the process is reversed, and the magnitude halves
because the equation is halved.
The positive sign makes sense — splitting water requires energy, which is why electrolysis
needs a power supply.
∴ +285.8 kJ.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|12||0|0:
Buna rubbers are named by a formula: **Bu** from the diene, **Na** from sodium, the catalyst
used in the original polymerisation, and a final letter for the comonomer.
So in Buna-S:
Bu = buta**diene**, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂
Na = sodium (natrium), the polymerisation catalyst
S = styrene, C₆H₅CH=CH₂
Buta-1,3-diene is essential because it has two double bonds: one is consumed in the 1,4-addition
polymerisation and the other remains in the chain, giving the elasticity and the sites for later
vulcanisation. A simple butene, with only one double bond, could not do this.
The same scheme names Buna-N, where N is acrylonitrile.
∴ Bu stands for butadiene.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|13||0|0:
Copper is one of the irregular configurations. Instead of [Ar]3d⁹4s², a filled d subshell is
more stable, so one 4s electron is promoted:
Cu (Z = 29) = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
Now form Cu²⁺ by removing two electrons. For transition metals the **4s electrons are removed
first**, before any 3d, because once the 3d orbitals are occupied they lie below 4s in energy.
Remove the single 4s electron ⇒ Cu⁺ = [Ar] 3d¹⁰
Remove one more, now necessarily from 3d ⇒ Cu²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s⁰
The lone unpaired electron in 3d⁹ is why Cu²⁺ salts are paramagnetic and coloured, while
Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰, fully filled) is diamagnetic and colourless.
Options (1), (3) and (4) all wrongly keep electrons in 4s.
∴ [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s⁰.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|15||0|0:
The electromeric effect is a **temporary** effect seen only while an attacking reagent is
present. The shared pair of a multiple bond is transferred completely to one of the two atoms:
>C=C< + reagent ⇒ >C⁺–C⁻<
The essential points are that it involves the **π electrons**, that it is complete rather than
partial, and that it disappears the moment the reagent is removed.
Compare it with the inductive effect, which is the *partial* displacement of **σ** electrons
along a chain and is permanent — that is what option (3) describes.
Option (2) is wrong because σ electrons are localised in the bond and are not delocalised, and
(4) wrongly adds σ electrons to the π ones.
Of the four, (1) is the one that correctly identifies π electrons as the ones involved.
∴ delocalisation of π-electrons.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|17||0|0:
The adsorption theory explains catalysis where the catalyst is a **solid** and the reactants
are gases or liquids — that is, heterogeneous catalysis.
The mechanism runs in five steps:
1. the reactant molecules diffuse to the catalyst surface
2. they are adsorbed on it, usually by chemisorption
3. adsorption weakens the bonds within the reactant, lowering the activation energy
4. the reaction occurs on the surface, where reactants are held close and correctly oriented
5. the products are desorbed, freeing the site for the next molecules
It explains two things neatly: why finely divided catalysts work best, since the effect depends
on surface area, and why catalysts are poisoned, since an impurity that occupies the active
sites blocks step 2.
Homogeneous catalysis has no surface, so adsorption cannot be involved; it is explained by the
intermediate compound formation theory instead.
∴ heterogeneous catalysis.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|18||0|0:
Ethane has two carbons and methane only one, so the carbon chain must be **lengthened**.
Step 1 — chlorinate the methane with Cl₂ in UV light, a free radical substitution:
CH₄ + Cl₂ ⇒ CH₃Cl + HCl
Step 2 — the Wurtz reaction couples two alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether:
2CH₃Cl + 2Na ⇒ CH₃–CH₃ + 2NaCl
The two methyl groups join, giving ethane ✓
Now see why the others fail.
(1) Alcoholic KOH eliminates HCl, but CH₃Cl has no β-hydrogen, so no alkene can form.
(2) Aqueous KOH substitutes to give methanol, CH₃OH — still one carbon.
(4) Decarboxylation *removes* a carbon, going the wrong way; and there is no acid to start from.
Only Wurtz joins two fragments, which is what doubling the chain requires.
∴ chlorination followed by the Wurtz reaction.
